name: Oxidative Thermal Drift Drone OTDD-4 'Ember'
description:
The OTDD-4 is a persistent area-heating platform developed by OUROBOROS ENERGY's defense subsidiary from industrial thermal management technology originally designed for pipeline thaw operations in extreme cold environments. The drone carries a focused oxidative catalytic emitter — a system that superheats a concentrated column of ambient air through rapid catalytic oxidation cycling rather than combustion, producing a sustained thermal cone that can raise surface temperatures in a 3-meter radius by 40–90 degrees Celsius depending on proximity and dwell time. The effect on organic targets ranges from rapid dehydration and heat exhaustion at range to contact burns and respiratory damage at close quarters.

The OTDD-4 is not a fast weapon. It moves slowly, holds altitude with deliberate stability, and requires 8–12 seconds of dwell time to produce incapacitating effects on an unprotected target. What it offers is persistence and silence — the catalytic emitter produces no flame, no visible beam, and no significant acoustic signature. Targets describe the experience as standing next to an industrial furnace that appeared from nowhere. The drone's thermal signature is, paradoxically, a liability: most military-grade thermal detection systems will acquire it immediately. It was designed for use against targets without such equipment.

OUROBOROS ENERGY's civilian documentation describes the OTDD-4 as an 'ice management and environmental thermal correction platform.' The same hardware, the same firmware, the same catalytic array. The company notes that operational parameters outside intended use cases are the operator's legal responsibility.
specifications:
dimensions: 40 cm diameter disc, 18 cm depth
weight: 2.3 kg
thermal output: 40–90°C surface temperature increase at target (proximity-dependent)
effective range: 0.5–4 m thermal cone
dwell time for incapacitation: 8–12 seconds (unprotected target)
flight ceiling: 30 m
battery life: 28 minutes at full thermal output
noise signature: < 22 dB at 5 m
visible emissions: None (no flame or visible beam)
thermal signature: Highly detectable on thermal optics
countermeasures: Thermal-rated suit (Class 3+), thermal detection equipment, distance
tactical_use: OTDD-4 units are used to flush targets from cover, deny enclosed spaces, and suppress movement without direct confrontation. Operators fly them into rooms ahead of entry teams, forcing occupants into the open or toward prepared positions. In outdoor contexts, they're used against targets in concealed positions who lack thermal detection capability. Extended dwell operations — hovering over a fixed position for the full 28-minute battery cycle — can render a room uninhabitable for hours afterward due to residual surface heat.
cultural_context: OUROBOROS ENERGY's dual-use strategy with the OTDD-4 is considered one of GLMZ's more brazen corporate maneuvers. The company openly sells the hardware through industrial supply channels, and the combat firmware is available on the black market for a modest premium. When confronted about documented combat deployments, OUROBOROS' communications team reliably notes that pipeline thaw operations can involve significant thermal output requirements. The drone has consequently become a symbol of corporate accountability theater — a favorite example cited by reform advocates and investigative journalists as evidence that GLMZ's legal distinctions between industrial and military hardware are functionally meaningless.
known_users: Mid-tier gang enforcers (black market firmware variant)
Corporate extraction teams operating against unequipped targets
story_hooks: An OUROBOROS ENERGY field technician was found dead in a pipeline maintenance access tunnel — cause of death, thermal exposure consistent with OTDD-4 dwell pattern. The company's own drone killed one of their own people, and the firmware logs have been wiped.

A community organizer in the Underbelly has been receiving OTDD-4 harassment — the drone appears outside her window at night, idles for twenty minutes, leaves. No contact burns, no property damage. Just heat. Just a reminder. The serial number traces to an OUROBOROS industrial supply account.

The party needs to cross a contested building that a well-funded crew has seeded with OTDD-4 units running loiter patterns. The building has no thermal detection equipment. The question is whether they go in blind and fast, or find another way.

physical_description.visual_profile: A flat, industrial disc hovering silently — part ceiling fan, part furnace. The OTDD-4 reads as a purposeful piece of thermal machinery scaled down to drone size. Its shape suggests stability over speed; wide stance, minimal protrusions. At rest, it looks inert. In operation, the air around it distorts.
physical_description.dimensions: 40 cm diameter disc, 18 cm depth (chassis). Catalytic emitter array extends 6 cm below fuselage.
physical_description.weight_description: Dense but manageable — 2.3 kg feels substantial in hand, suggests high-grade materials and internal thermal plumbing. Not light, not unwieldy. Balanced weight distribution.
physical_description.primary_material: Brushed titanium alloy chassis with embedded copper thermal cycling channels visible as fine lines across the disc surface. Underslung catalytic emitter housing is hardened polymer composite, heat-treated to dull bronze.
physical_description.finish: Matte titanium-grey on the primary disc with oxidation staining around the emitter vents — rust-colored thermal scarring from operational heat bleed. Copper channels show a deliberate brushed pattern that catches light.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal grey primary with burnt copper accents. The emitter housing transitions from charcoal to deep rust-orange at the heat vents. Minimal branding colors.
physical_description.grip_texture: Recessed grip points on the disc perimeter lined with textured silicone — non-slip, heat-resistant. Cool to the touch even after operation.
distinctive_features: Copper thermal cycling channels etched in visible lines across the top surface
Recessed emitter array underneath with honeycomb heat dissipation grille
Three flush-mount indicator LEDs (status, thermal load, battery) in a subtle triangle near the edge
Hairline thermal stress fractures in the polymer emitter housing from repeated use
Asymmetrical rotor arrangement — four rotors positioned off-center for stable hover over hot columns
Heat-reactive paint showing operation history as faint purple zones where temperatures peaked
Diagnostic port on the side rim (OUROBOROS proprietary connector)
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: OUROBOROS ENERGY logomark stamped in the center of the top surface (slightly recessed to avoid snag). Model number OTDD-4 etched along the rim in small, professional lettering. Serial plate on the side (thermal-resistant adhesive label, partially heat-damaged on field units).
physical_description.condition_typical: Well-maintained examples show the intentional wear — thermal scarring, dust buildup around the emitter grille, slight discoloration from repeated heat cycling. Black-market combat-tuned units often show stress fractures or evidence of firmware modification (small solder points visible near the processor access panel). Civilian units look cleaner, almost sterile.
